questions.stem: Which are the two main types of white blood cell?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Neither is a white cell.
Both are fluid fractions.
Both belong to clotting.

questions.stem: What is phagocytosis?

options.explanation: That belongs to red cells.

options.text: The engulfing and digestion of pathogens by phagocytes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is lymphocyte work.
Clotting involves platelets and fibrin.

questions.stem: How do phagocytes find their targets?

options.explanation: Sugar sensing is not the mechanism.
Antibodies assist later; detection is chemical.

options.text: Their sensitive cell surface membrane detects chemicals produced by pathogens
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Cells do not see.

questions.stem: What do phagocytes release once a pathogen is engulfed?

options.explanation: Those come from lymphocytes.
Nothing of the sort is released.
No bubbling occurs.

options.text: Digestive enzymes that break it down
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: Why is phagocytosis called a non-specific response?

options.text: It acts against any pathogen, without targeting one particular type
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because it fails against most pathogens
options.explanation: It works broadly, which is its strength.

options.text: Because only one pathogen triggers it
options.explanation: Any pathogen's chemicals can trigger it.
Speed is not what non-specific means.

questions.stem: State what phagocytes do to pathogens.
questions.modelAnswer: They engulf the pathogen and digest it with released enzymes.

questions.stem: Name the response type of phagocytosis.
questions.modelAnswer: Phagocytosis is a non-specific immune response.

questions.stem: Explain why chemical detection suits the phagocyte's role.
questions.modelAnswer: Because chemicals leak from any invading pathogen, a chemical trigger lets the phagocyte catch every invader early without needing to identify its species.

questions.stem: Pus collects at a wound. Explain its composition in white-cell terms.
questions.modelAnswer: Pus is largely dead phagocytes that engulfed pathogens, mixed with the destroyed material they digested.

questions.stem: What is an antigen?

options.text: A type of white blood cell
options.explanation: Antigens are molecules, not cells.

options.text: A surface marker that the body treats as foreign
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
That is an antibody.
Digestion products are not antigens by definition.

questions.stem: What shape relationship makes an antibody fit its antigen?

options.explanation: The fit is specific, not random.
Mismatched shapes cannot bind.

options.text: Complementary — the antibody's shape matches that specific antigen
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Complementary means matching shapes, not identical ones.

questions.stem: Why is the lymphocyte response called specific?

options.explanation: Non-specific belongs to phagocytes.
Speed is not what specific means.
They target the foreign markers.

options.text: Each antibody fits only one type of antigen
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: What do lymphocytes do to raise antibody numbers quickly?

options.text: They clone themselves into many lymphocytes making the same antibody
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Engulfing is phagocyte work.
Shrinking helps nothing.
No such conversion exists.

questions.stem: Which two sources give a person immunity?

options.explanation: Those are barriers, not immunity in this sense.

options.text: Enough antibodies already present, or memory cells that produce antibodies rapidly
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Neither grants immunity directly.
Neither defines immunity.

questions.stem: Distinguish antigen from antibody.
questions.modelAnswer: An antigen sits on a cell's outer surface; an antibody is the matching protein a lymphocyte builds against it.

questions.stem: State what antibodies do once attached to pathogens.
questions.modelAnswer: They clump the pathogens together and mark them for destruction.

questions.stem: Explain why one lymphocyte cannot serve two different pathogens.
questions.modelAnswer: Because its antibody is shaped to one antigen's shape, and a different pathogen's markers do not fit, so only a matching lineage can respond.

questions.stem: A patient recovers from a viral infection. Explain their immunity afterwards.
questions.modelAnswer: The response left antibodies and memory lymphocytes specific to that virus, so a re-infection meets antibodies already present and a rapid memory-cell surge.

questions.stem: What happens first in the infection sequence?

options.explanation: Clearance is the final step.
Symptoms follow toxin release and cell infection.

options.text: The pathogen enters the bloodstream and multiplies
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Recognition comes later in the sequence.

questions.stem: Which event causes the patient's symptoms?

options.explanation: Antibodies fight; they do not cause symptoms.
Engulfment is protective.
Cloning is part of the defence.

options.text: Release of toxins and infection of body cells
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which cells act FIRST against the invading pathogen?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
They join after the pathogen is encountered and recognised.
Platelets clot wounds, not infections.
They carry oxygen, not defence.

questions.stem: What triggers the lymphocyte's antibody production?

options.explanation: Toxins cause symptoms; antigens trigger recognition.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Fever is a symptom, not the trigger.
Digestion may present fragments, but recognition is of antigens.

questions.stem: How are destroyed pathogens finally removed?

options.explanation: Lymphocytes produce antibodies; phagocytes clear.
Excretion is not the immune sequence's step.

options.text: Phagocytes engulf and digest the marked remains
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Clearance is cellular, not chemical.

questions.stem: State the role of antibody binding in the sequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Antibodies recognise and bind the pathogens, marking them for destruction.

questions.stem: Name the two phases of the immune response in order.
questions.modelAnswer: The non-specific phagocyte response comes first, then the specific lymphocyte and antibody response.

questions.stem: Explain why the pathogen multiplies before the body feels ill.
questions.modelAnswer: Because symptoms arise from toxin release and cell infection, which take time to build as the pathogen multiplies first in the bloodstream.

questions.stem: A second infection by the same bacterium meets which shortcuts compared with the first?
questions.modelAnswer: Memory lymphocytes recognise the antigens at once, so antibody production begins sooner, in greater quantity, and the phagocytes clear the marked bacteria faster.
